gangani-britain.t: People of the Llŷn peninsula in north-west Wales, known from a headland Ptolemy named after them, with namesakes in western Ireland.
gangani-britain.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 names a Ganganorum Promontorium, the headland of the Gangani, on the coast of north-west Wales, generally identified with the tip of the Llŷn peninsula. Ptolemy does not list the Gangani among the inland peoples, so they may have been a small coastal group or a subdivision of the Ordovices.
gangani-britain.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society. Llŷn was a land of hillforts such as Tre'r Ceiri, a stone-walled settlement occupied into the Roman period, and of farming and fishing communities. The identical name in Ireland, borne by the Gangani (Ireland) on the Shannon, has prompted theories of migration across the Irish Sea in either direction.
gangani-britain.e: The Gangani are not mentioned again. Llŷn later saw Irish settlement in the post-Roman period and became part of the Kingdom of Gwynedd.

grand-duchy-of-luxembourg.t: The world's only remaining grand duchy, created in 1815 and grown from a fortress state into a founding member of the European Union and a financial centre.
grand-duchy-of-luxembourg.o: The Congress of Vienna made the former Duchy of Luxembourg a grand duchy, held by William I of the Netherlands in personal union and a member of the German Confederation, with a Prussian garrison in its fortress. After the Belgian Revolution, the Treaty of London of 1839 gave its French-speaking western half to Belgium.
grand-duchy-of-luxembourg.r: The Treaty of London of 1867 made Luxembourg permanently neutral and its fortress was demolished. Personal union with the Netherlands ended in 1890, when Adolphe of Nassau-Weilburg became grand duke. Steel, based on local iron ore, made the country prosperous. Germany occupied it in both world wars, and Grand Duchess Charlotte led resistance from exile.
grand-duchy-of-luxembourg.e: After 1945 Luxembourg abandoned neutrality, co-founding Benelux, NATO and the European Communities and hosting European institutions. As steel declined it became a banking and investment centre. It remains a constitutional monarchy; Grand Duke Guillaume succeeded his father Henri in 2025.

gela.t: Rhodian and Cretan colony on Sicily's south coast whose tyrants, Hippocrates and Gelon, built the first great Greek power on the island.
gela.o: Colonists from Lindos on Rhodes and from Crete, led by Antiphemus and Entimus, founded Gela around 689 BCE on a long ridge by the Gela river, inland of a sandy coast. The colony pushed into the Sicel interior and in 580 BCE founded Acragas to the west.
gela.r: Gela reached its peak under the tyrants Cleander and Hippocrates, who around 495 BCE dominated much of eastern Sicily, and under Gelon, who seized Syracuse in 485 BCE and moved half of Gela's people there. Its farmland produced grain and horses, and its terracotta workshops and coins with a man-headed bull were renowned. The playwright Aeschylus died there in 456 BCE.
gela.e: Carthage sacked Gela in 405 BCE. Timoleon resettled it in the 330s BCE, but in 282 BCE Phintias, tyrant of Acragas, destroyed it and moved its people to his new city at Licata. The site was refounded by Frederick II in 1233 as Terranova, renamed Gela in 1927.

gadir.t: The great Phoenician city of Cádiz, gateway to the Atlantic, home of a famous temple of Melqart and one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Europe.
gadir.o: Gadir was founded by settlers from Tyre on islands off the Atlantic coast near the mouth of the Guadalete. Ancient writers dated its foundation to around 1100 BCE, but archaeology places it in the 9th to 8th centuries BCE. Its position beyond the Strait of Gibraltar gave access to Tartessian silver and Atlantic tin.
gadir.r: Gadir was governed by its own elite under institutions modelled on Tyre, and its temple of Melqart, later identified with Hercules, drew pilgrims from across the Mediterranean; Hannibal visited before marching on Italy in 218 BCE. Fish salting, purple dye and long-distance trade made it rich, and it came to lead the Phoenician towns of the south under Carthaginian hegemony.
gadir.e: In 206 BCE, after the Carthaginian defeat at Ilipa, Gadir went over to Rome under a treaty of alliance. Its citizens received Roman citizenship under Julius Caesar, and Gades became one of the wealthiest cities of Hispania Baetica.

generalitat-of-catalonia-1931-1939.t: Catalonia's autonomous government under the Second Republic, restored after two centuries and abolished after Franco's victory.
generalitat-of-catalonia-1931-1939.o: On 14 April 1931 Francesc Macià of the Republican Left of Catalonia proclaimed a Catalan Republic in Barcelona. After negotiations with Madrid it became an autonomous government that took the medieval name of the Generalitat, and the Statute of Autonomy was approved in 1932.
generalitat-of-catalonia-1931-1939.r: The Generalitat had its own parliament and powers over education, culture, public order and civil law, and promoted the Catalan language. Lluís Companys succeeded Macià in 1933. In October 1934 Companys proclaimed a Catalan State within a federal republic, leading to his arrest and the statute's suspension until 1936. During the civil war it ran much of the Republican war effort in Catalonia.
generalitat-of-catalonia-1931-1939.e: Nationalist forces took Barcelona in January 1939, and Franco abolished the autonomy. Companys was handed over by the Gestapo and executed in 1940. The Generalitat survived in exile and was restored in 1977.

gallaecia.t: The late Roman province of north-western Iberia, created by Diocletian and soon to become the home of the Suebic kingdom.
gallaecia.o: Gallaecia was formed around 293 by Diocletian's reform, which split Hispania Tarraconensis into smaller provinces. It covered the lands of the Callaeci and Astures, from the Douro to the Bay of Biscay, with Bracara Augusta (Braga) as its capital.
gallaecia.r: A governor ran the province under the Diocese of Hispania. Its economy was rural, based on farming, herding and the remains of the gold-mining industry around Asturica Augusta. Towns such as Lucus Augusti (Lugo), with its surviving walls, were fortified in the late 3rd century. Christianity spread, and the ascetic movement of Priscillian, executed in 385, found strong support here.
gallaecia.e: In 409 Suebi and Hasding Vandals entered Gallaecia, and the Suebi made it the centre of their kingdom. Roman rule faded, as recorded by Hydatius, bishop of Aquae Flaviae, and the name lived on in the medieval Kingdom of Galicia.

gangani-ireland.t: People of western Ireland recorded by Ptolemy near the Shannon estuary, sharing their name with the Gangani of north-west Wales.
gangani-ireland.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 places the Gangani on the west coast of Ireland, south of the Auteini and north of the Velabri, usually located in County Clare or around the mouth of the Shannon. The same name is given to a headland in Wales, home of the Gangani (Britain), on the Llŷn peninsula.
gangani-ireland.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or customs. The shared name on both sides of the Irish Sea has been taken as evidence of migration, of an Irish group settled in Wales, or simply of a common Celtic word, perhaps connected with Irish legends of the Gamanrad, but none of these ideas can be proven.
gangani-ireland.e: The Gangani of Ireland do not appear in later sources. Their region later formed part of the Kingdom of Munster and the lands of peoples such as the Ui Fidgenti.

gibraltar.t: A British territory on the rock at the entrance to the Mediterranean, held since 1704 and still claimed by Spain.
gibraltar.o: An Anglo-Dutch fleet under Admiral George Rooke captured Gibraltar in 1704 during the War of the Spanish Succession, nominally for the Habsburg claimant Charles. Spain ceded the town and fortress to Great Britain in perpetuity by Article X of the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713.
gibraltar.r: Gibraltar became a fortress and naval base guarding the Strait, surviving the Great Siege of 1779-1783 and serving as a key base in the Napoleonic and World Wars. Its mixed population of Genoese, Spanish, Maltese, Jewish and British origin developed a distinct identity and the Llanito speech. It became a Crown colony in 1830.
gibraltar.e: Spain pressed its claim at the UN; Gibraltarians voted to stay British in 1967, and Spain closed the land border from 1969 to 1985. In 2002 they rejected shared sovereignty. Today it is a self-governing British Overseas Territory, with its border regime negotiated after Brexit.

getae.t: Thracian people of the lower Danube, followers of the god Zalmoxis, whose king Dromichaetes captured Lysimachus and whose lands formed the core of Dacia.
getae.o: Herodotus names the Getae among Thracians living south and north of the lower Danube when Darius I marched against the Scythians around 514 BCE; they alone resisted before being subdued. Their territory covered the Danube plain in modern Bulgaria and Romania.
getae.r: Getic chiefs and kings ruled from fortified centres; the royal city of Helis is often identified with Sveshtari, where a decorated tomb survives. Herodotus says the Getae believed in immortality through the god Zalmoxis. Grain, horses and trade with Greek Black Sea cities such as Histria shaped the economy. Around 292 BCE King Dromichaetes defeated and captured Lysimachus, then released him.
getae.e: Celtic incursions and pressure from Macedon and Rome fragmented Getic power. About 82 BCE Burebista united the Getae and Dacians into the Kingdom of Dacia; Roman writers afterwards used Getae and Dacians almost interchangeably.

galindians.t: The southernmost Baltic people of Prussia, living among the Masurian lakes and named by Ptolemy, whose land was almost empty by the time the Teutonic Knights arrived.
galindians.o: Ptolemy listed the Galindai in the 2nd century, and they are usually located in the lake country of southern Prussia, roughly modern Masuria in Poland. Like their neighbours the Sudovians and other Prussian groups, they lived in scattered clans around fortified hilltops, without any known central authority.
galindians.r: Almost nothing is recorded of their institutions. They farmed, fished and hunted in a land of forest and lakes, and shared the pagan religion and West Baltic speech of the Prussians. The Teutonic chronicler Peter of Dusburg claimed that Galindia had been depopulated by wars and famine long before his time.
galindians.e: By the late 13th century the area formed part of the great wilderness that the Teutonic Order absorbed during its conquest of Prussia, completed in 1283. Survivors were merged into the Prussian population, and the region was later resettled by German and Polish (Masurian) colonists.

gabali.t: Mountain people of the Lozère, clients of the Arverni, who gave their name to the Gévaudan.
gabali.o: The Gabali lived on the granite plateaus and valleys of the southern Massif Central, in the modern Lozère. Caesar names them as clients of the Arverni.
gabali.r: Pliny mentions their silver mines and their cheese, which was sold in Rome. No rulers or institutions are recorded.
gabali.e: They took part in the revolt of Vercingetorix in 52 BCE, attacking the Helvii on the border of the Province. Under Rome their chief town was Anderitum (Javols), and their name lived on in the medieval county and bishopric of Gévaudan.

genoese-famagusta.t: Genoese-held enclave around the great port of Famagusta in Cyprus, seized from the Lusignan kings in 1373 and held for ninety years.
genoese-famagusta.o: At the coronation of King Peter II of Cyprus in Famagusta in 1372, a dispute over precedence between Genoese and Venetian merchants led to riots in which Genoese were killed. Genoa sent a fleet in 1373, invaded the Kingdom of Cyprus and occupied Famagusta, keeping the city as security for a huge indemnity.
genoese-famagusta.r: Genoa governed Famagusta through a podesta and officials, and from 1447 through the Bank of Saint George, which ran it as a business. The once-thriving port declined as Genoa restricted the trade of the rest of the island and Mamluk and Turkish pressure grew. Many inhabitants left and the economy shrank.
genoese-famagusta.e: King James II of Cyprus, with Mamluk support, besieged Famagusta and recovered it in 1464, reuniting the island under the Lusignans. Its Gothic cathedral of Saint Nicholas and walls remain.

golden-ambrosian-republic.t: A short-lived Milanese republic proclaimed when the Visconti line ended in 1447, which fell to its own general Francesco Sforza.
golden-ambrosian-republic.o: When Duke Filippo Maria Visconti died without a male heir in August 1447, a group of Milanese nobles and lawyers proclaimed a republic named after the city's patron saint Ambrose. Many subject cities of the Duchy of Milan seized the chance to break away.
golden-ambrosian-republic.r: The republic was led by elected captains and defenders of liberty, but split between nobles and popular leaders. Threatened by the Republic of Venice, it hired Francesco Sforza, husband of the late duke's illegitimate daughter Bianca Maria, who defeated the Venetians at Caravaggio in 1448. Sforza then made a separate peace with Venice and turned against Milan.
golden-ambrosian-republic.e: Sforza besieged the city, and in February 1450, with Milan starving, the citizens opened the gates. He was acclaimed duke, restoring the Duchy of Milan under the Sforza dynasty.

gortyn.t: Powerful city of the Mesara in southern Crete, famous for the Gortyn Code, the longest surviving early Greek law inscription.
gortyn.o: Gortyn grew in the early Iron Age on the Lethaios river at the western edge of the Mesara plain, near the older Minoan centre of Phaistos. By the 7th century BCE it was a Dorian city and, with Knossos, one of the two strongest powers on Crete.
gortyn.r: The Gortyn Code, inscribed c. 450 BCE on a wall later built into the Roman odeion, sets out laws on marriage, divorce, inheritance, adoption and the status of slaves and serfs. Gortyn was ruled by kosmoi magistrates and had men's messes. In the Hellenistic period it fought Knossos and destroyed Phaistos c. 150 BCE.
gortyn.e: After the Roman conquest of 69 to 67 BCE, Gortyn, which had cooperated with Rome, became the capital of the province of Crete and Cyrenaica. It flourished under the Empire and the early Byzantines.

gallic-empire.t: Breakaway Roman state in Gaul, Britain and for a time Hispania, set up by Postumus in 260 when the empire seemed unable to defend its frontiers.
gallic-empire.o: In 260, after the emperor Valerian was captured by the Persians and Germanic invaders broke across the Rhine, the governor Postumus was proclaimed emperor by his troops at Cologne. He killed Gallienus' son Saloninus and won the loyalty of Gaul, Germania, Britain and Hispania.
gallic-empire.r: The Gallic emperors kept Roman institutions, with their own consuls, praetorian guard and mints at Cologne and Trier. They did not march on Rome but concentrated on defending the Rhine. Postumus was murdered by his troops in 269, followed by Marius, Victorinus and Tetricus I.
gallic-empire.e: Hispania returned to the central empire early, and Victorinus was murdered in 271. In 274 Aurelian defeated Tetricus near Châlons, where Tetricus seems to have abandoned his army. He was paraded in Aurelian's triumph and then given an office in Italy, and the provinces rejoined the Roman Empire.

grand-duchy-of-tuscany.t: The Medici and then Habsburg-Lorraine state of Tuscany, patron of Galileo and a pioneer of Enlightenment reform, including abolition of the death penalty.
grand-duchy-of-tuscany.o: In 1569 Pope Pius V raised Cosimo I de' Medici, ruler of the Duchy of Florence and conqueror of Siena, to the rank of Grand Duke of Tuscany, a title confirmed by the emperor in 1576.
grand-duchy-of-tuscany.r: The Medici grand dukes ran a centralised state from Florence. Ferdinando I made Livorno a free port open to Jews and foreign merchants, and Cosimo II made Galileo court mathematician. The Medici line ended in 1737; the last heiress, Anna Maria Luisa, left the family's art collections to Florence. Francis Stephen of Lorraine succeeded, and his son Peter Leopold reformed law and trade, abolishing torture and the death penalty in 1786.
grand-duchy-of-tuscany.e: Napoleon turned Tuscany into the Kingdom of Etruria in 1801 and annexed it to France in 1807. Restored in 1814, the Lorraine dynasty left when Leopold II fled in 1859, and Tuscany voted to join the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1860.

great-moravia.t: The first major Slavic state in central Europe, where Cyril and Methodius created a Slavic liturgy and alphabet that shaped the Orthodox Slavic world.
great-moravia.o: Around 833 Prince Mojmír I of the Moravians drove Pribina out of Nitra and united the Slavs north of the middle Danube, creating a state centred on the Morava valley. Mojmír's successor Rastislav, installed with East Frankish help in 846, soon turned against East Francia and built a strong independent principality.
great-moravia.r: Great Moravia's power rested on large fortified centres such as Mikulčice, Staré Město and Pohansko, with stone churches and rich graves. In 863 Rastislav invited the Byzantine brothers Cyril and Methodius, who created the Glagolitic alphabet and Old Church Slavonic liturgy. Under Svatopluk I, the realm expanded into Bohemia, southern Poland and Pannonia.
great-moravia.e: After Svatopluk died in 894 his sons quarrelled and Bohemia broke away. Magyar invasions destroyed Great Moravia around 906 to 907; the last mention coincides with the Battle of Pressburg in 907. Its disciples carried the Slavic liturgy to Bulgaria, while its lands passed to the Duchy of Bohemia and Hungary.
